source.title: Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off
source.authors: Mikhail Belkin; Daniel J. Hsu; Si-Yuan Ma; Soumik Mandal

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically sweeps model capacity and measures test risk across neural networks, feature models, and ensemble methods. Its methods differ across model families, and the paper itself presents the generalized double-descent finding.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-risk curves from its own capacity sweeps. It also reports training risks and norm curves, but the rows below focus on test risk. The stated epoch schedules are setup details, not results about test error over epochs. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: This is one of the claim's original sources (arXiv:1812.11118). It runs its own capacity sweeps and reports test risk for RFF, Random ReLU features, one-hidden-layer networks, random forests, L2-boosting and a synthetic model. Because it is an original source, it gets no verdict labels.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as stated. The authors also argue that double descent is ubiquitous. They say regularization and early stopping can mask the peak, and that the peak for neural networks lies in a narrow parameter range.
record.recipe_differences: This paper reports its own capacity sweeps across feature models, neural networks, trees, and synthetic models; it is not a reproduction of the original study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that high shrinkage (parameter value 0.1) makes the L2-boosting curve less apparent than shrinkage 0.85. Neural-network behavior also has greater variance without weight reuse.

fits_no_version.finding: The ℓ2 norm of the learned predictor peaks at the interpolation threshold and decreases beyond it, for RFF, Random ReLU features and the synthetic model. The authors posit this as the mechanism behind the second descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The norm of the minimum-norm interpolating predictor peaks at the interpolation threshold and falls as capacity grows, tracking the second descent.

record.problems: Most reported test-risk curves are figure-only, without numeric values or uncertainty intervals. Neural-network optimization is sensitive to initialization; the paper reports greater variance without weight reuse. RFF and Random ReLU results are based on a single run, while neural-network and ensemble experiments are repeated five times.
record.rows_left_out: Training-risk and norm curves are not separately extracted because the claim versions concern test risk. No separately reported test-risk results beyond the listed capacity sweeps were omitted.

untested.parts: Deep (multi-layer) networks. Only one-hidden-layer fully connected networks are tested.
All of it. No test-risk curve over epochs is reported.
All of it. Sample size is varied only in the synthetic model, with 'results similar'. No sample-wise non-monotonicity is reported.
All of it. No single complexity measure is shown to predict the peak's location across size, epoch and sample axes.
Whether label noise drives the peak, multiple or triple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
All of it. No re-indexing by an effective parameter count is done.

missing.what: Synthetic-model sweeps at other sample sizes (n from 2^6 to 2^11), reported as giving similar double-descent curves.
Norm curves that peak at N=n and then decrease. These are left out as non-test-risk, but they carry the paper's mechanism argument.

record.verdict_notes: This paper is an original source for the claim, so no verdict labels are given. It was reclassed from T2 to T1 because it defines the original method. Most results are figure-only. RFF and Random ReLU runs are single runs, while network and ensemble results are means of five runs. For trees and boosting, 'capacity' is a hybrid index (leaves, then number of trees or forests), which bears on how complexity is counted (V7) but does not test it.

versions.untested_parts: The neural-network tests use fully connected networks with a single hidden layer; they do not establish the claim for deep networks generally.
No test-risk curve over training epochs is reported.
The paper varies sample size in synthetic experiments but does not report whether increasing training samples near the interpolation threshold raises test risk.
The experiments cover the model families and datasets described in the rows, not all model classes.
The paper discusses and measures norm behavior in some settings, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location along size, epoch, and sample axes.
The synthetic experiment compares SNR = ∞ and SNR = 20, and the paper reports an attenuation under high shrinkage. It does not test multiple or triple peaks or optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not recast the curve using an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
